proposedDescription: Canterbury bells usually spends its first year as a leafy rosette, then sends up a tall stem lined with generous bell-shaped flowers. Blue, pink, purple and white garden forms make this European biennial a familiar cottage-garden plant. The lower leaves are long and toothed, with smaller leaves along the flowering stem. Seed escapes through small openings in the dry capsules, allowing new plants to appear nearby. Deadhead before capsules mature if you want to keep the display within its chosen bed.
identification: Look for a basal rosette of toothed leaves and an upright stem bearing large bell-shaped flowers; cultivated forms may be double.
actions: Remove spent flower stems before seed release if self-sowing is unwanted, and check nearby beds for seedlings.
researchNotes: Garden escape profile; national invasive impacts not established by consulted floras.

claims: Biennial forms a first-year rosette and second-year flower stem; capsules release small seeds; deadheading limits reseeding.
Botanical account describes leaves, large bell-shaped corollas and occurrence outside cultivation.

proposedDescription: Cape blue waterlily holds its fragrant flowers above a raft of broad floating leaves. Although blue is the familiar color, named forms and cultivated relatives can also flower pink or mauve. The leaves have a deep notch and a wavy edge, while a short upright, tuberous rhizome anchors the plant below. It comes from Africa and grows in still or slow water. Keep pond plants and discarded rhizomes out of natural waterways, and use more than flower color to distinguish this species from waterlily hybrids.
identification: Photograph floating leaf margins and the raised flower, including its colored anther tips; rhizome form helps specialists distinguish similar waterlilies.
actions: Contain pond plantings and dispose of unwanted rhizomes away from waterways; obtain specialist identification before managing a wild stand.
researchNotes: NZ Flora explicitly contrasts traditional N. capensis with the broader N. nouchali var. caerulea treatment. Catalog ID retained; no hybrid equivalence assumed.

claims: African aquatic perennial has floating wavy leaves, flowers above water and upright tuberous rhizomes; hybrids and taxonomic treatments complicate identification.
Perennial has small tubers developing into short vertical rhizomes; botanical flower and leaf characters described.

proposedDescription: Cape honeysuckle is a scrambling southern African shrub with clusters of bright trumpet flowers. It belongs to the trumpetvine family, and its compound leaves—usually with five to nine toothed leaflets—help distinguish it from true honeysuckles. Orange-red is typical, with yellow and other colors available in garden selections. Long capsules release winged seeds, and stems can be propagated by layering or cuttings. Give a planting room, prune it to the intended space, and keep rooted trimmings from being dumped beyond the garden.
identification: Look for opposite compound leaves with toothed leaflets, tubular orange-red flowers and long narrow seed capsules.
actions: Manage the plant's spread by pruning and checking for rooted stems or seedlings; contain discarded cuttings.
researchNotes: Modern sources use Tecomaria capensis, with Tecoma capensis as synonym. Catalog ID retained; no nationwide invasive assertion.

claims: Southern African shrub or vine has 5–9 leaflets, trumpet flowers and wind-dispersed seeds; layering propagates plants.
Opposite pinnate leaves and terminal orange-red flower clusters characterize the scrambling shrub.

proposedDescription: Cape leadwort is a loose, scrambling shrub covered in clusters of pale blue flowers, with white-flowered selections also grown. Its small light-green leaves have little ear-shaped appendages near the base, a useful detail behind the name auriculata. Native to southern Africa, it is widely planted in warm gardens and can become a broad mass without pruning. Sunny conditions and good drainage suit it well. Keep a planting within its intended area and collect trimmings rather than dropping them at the edge of natural vegetation.
identification: Check for rounded clusters of five-lobed pale blue flowers and small leaves with ear-like basal appendages on scrambling stems.
actions: Prune to maintain the intended boundary, use well-drained sites, and keep discarded plant material out of natural areas.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Cape leadwort is a southern African shrub with pale blue or white flowers and spreading growth.
Leaves have ear-shaped appendages; shrub scrambles and flowers in rounded terminal clusters; it dislikes waterlogging.

proposedDescription: Fairy crassula spreads as a low succulent mat, with fleshy rounded leaves and airy clusters of small pale pink stars. Tiny plantlets may form among the flowers, drop to the ground, and become new plants; creeping stems also root where they touch soil. That easy propagation makes garden waste an effective way to start another patch. The South African species has become an environmental weed in parts of Australia and New Zealand. Collect every loose piece during removal and revisit the site for rooted fragments or fallen plantlets.
identification: Rounded fleshy leaves are dotted with pale or reddish pores; loose flower clusters can carry miniature plantlets.
actions: Contain cuttings and plantlets, remove rooted stems carefully, and monitor for regrowth rather than leaving fragments on bare soil.
researchNotes: Detailed sources treat subsp. multicava; description does not extend local seed observations to every population.

claims: Creeping stems root at nodes; pale pink star flowers are often replaced by plantlets; dense cover spreads vegetatively.
South African plant is an environmental weed spreading into Australian woodland and coastal vegetation.

proposedDescription: Cape ricegrass is easiest to notice when its seed heads develop long, twisted awns. These bristles give the annual grass a tangled appearance and help its sharp seeds catch on clothing or animal fur. Narrow leaves and a compact seed head support identification, but flowering material is especially useful. In southern California desert areas, it can form dense patches and is a concern for native wildflowers and fire potential. Brush seeds from footwear before leaving a patch and report unfamiliar stands to the local land manager.
identification: Look for an annual tuft of narrow leaves with dense panicles and very long, twice-bent, twisted awns.
actions: Clean seeds from clothing and equipment; document new patches and remove small plants before seed maturity where authorized.

proposedDescription: Cape ivy can drape a streambank or woodland edge in a thick green blanket. Its fleshy, lobed leaves resemble ivy, but clusters of tiny yellow flower heads reveal its place in the daisy family. In invaded coastal California habitats, the vine climbs over shrubs and trees and shades the plants beneath. Even small stem and underground pieces can start again after removal. Keep cut material out of waterways, collect fragments carefully, and expect repeated visits to clear regrowth rather than a single successful pull.
identification: Glossy fleshy leaves have five to seven pointed lobes; small clustered yellow flower heads lack the showy ray petals of some similar vines.
actions: Contain all fragments, protect nearby native plants during removal, and arrange repeated follow-up, especially near streams.

proposedDescription: Fertile capeweed spreads a rosette of deeply lobed leaves close to the ground, then lifts yellow daisy heads with dark centers above it. Turn a leaf over to see the pale, woolly underside. This seed-producing species is an agricultural and environmental weed in parts of Australia and has established in coastal California. Its seeds travel with soil, equipment, footwear, and animals. Remove small plants before seed ripens and check the identification carefully: the creeping ornamental capeweed, Arctotheca prostrata, has different spreading habits and yellow flower centers.
identification: Look for low lobed leaf rosettes with woolly white undersides and yellow rays surrounding a dark purple center.
actions: Prevent seed production, clean soil and seeds from equipment, and distinguish it from creeping A. prostrata before planning control.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Lobed leaves have woolly undersides; flowers have dark centers; spread is by seed carried with soil, animals and equipment.

proposedDescription: Creeping capeweed was planted as a groundcover for its low rosettes and cheerful yellow daisies, but its runners can cross the intended boundary. Stems root as they creep, allowing a patch to expand even where the cultivated plants produce no fertile seed. California records describe escapes into coastal prairie and nearby urban ground. It is often confused with fertile capeweed, Arctotheca calendula; longer creeping stems and yellow flower centers help separate it. During removal, collect rooted runners and fragments so the cleared patch can stay clear.
identification: Check for long creeping stems and flower heads with yellow centers; fertile A. calendula usually has dark centers.
actions: Avoid planting where it escapes locally; remove rooted runners, contain fragments and recheck the patch for regrowth.
researchNotes: Sterility qualified to cultivated material described in California, not asserted for every population. Second source is an explicit diagnostic comparison within the related-species account.

claims: Cultivated infertile capeweed escapes via creeping stolons into California coastal habitats.

proposedDescription: Capybaras are the largest living rodents, with sturdy brown bodies, blunt muzzles, and short legs adapted to life beside water. Partly webbed feet and eyes, ears, and nostrils set high on the head help them swim while keeping watch. In their South American range, they live socially and graze on grasses and aquatic plants. An animal seen far outside that range may be an escape or release. Observe from a distance, keep pets away, and report the location to wildlife authorities rather than feeding or relocating it.
identification: A large brown rodent with a barrel-shaped body, blunt head, no visible tail and partly webbed feet; do not confuse young animals with nutria.
actions: Do not feed, approach closely or release captive animals; document unexpected sightings and contact local wildlife authorities.
researchNotes: No established invasive population or local ecological impact inferred from isolated nonnative sightings.

claims: South American semiaquatic social herbivore has webbed feet and grazes near water.
Largest living rodent has a barrel-shaped body and high-set sensory organs suited to swimming.

proposedDescription: Wigandia is a large-leaved shrub or small tree from tropical America, with showy lavender flowers above coarse, hairy foliage. The hairs are a reason to admire it without brushing past: they can irritate skin and sometimes provoke a stronger allergic reaction. Plants described from the Santa Monica Mountains have escaped cultivation into dense colonies near homes. Their big, toothed leaves and curling flower clusters give a useful starting point for identification, although local forms and older botanical names need careful comparison.
identification: Look for large alternate leaves with toothed, wavy edges, conspicuous veins beneath and dense hairs, plus lavender, five-lobed flowers. The detailed California account concerns var. caracasana; confirm the local taxon.
actions: Photograph leaves and flowers without touching the hairs. Wear protective clothing if handling is necessary, avoid relocating plants from escaped colonies, and seek local advice on established patches.

proposedDescription: Caraway is the familiar kitchen spice grown on a delicate-looking member of the carrot family. Finely divided leaves form below branched stems topped with small white or pink-tinged flower umbels; the aromatic, ridged fruits are commonly called seeds. It often grows as a biennial and can self-sow freely where conditions suit it. In a herb bed, harvest or remove ripening heads to limit volunteers. Wild carrot-family plants can be difficult to tell apart, so do not use a casual resemblance as a basis for foraging.
identification: Look for finely divided leaves, small compound umbels and narrow ridged aromatic fruits; a full botanical identification is needed for a wild plant.
actions: Harvest or remove seed heads to limit self-sowing, and keep uncertain wild Apiaceae out of food preparations.

proposedDescription: Cardoon brings the artichoke family’s bold outline to open ground: a broad rosette of deeply cut, gray-green leaves sends up tall stems topped with purple flower heads. This Mediterranean perennial is cultivated as a vegetable and ornamental, but wild plants also occupy California grasslands and other disturbed habitats. Its spiny leaves and substantial taproot make established plants awkward to remove. Seed and surviving root pieces can renew a patch, so a single cut rarely settles the problem.
identification: Very large, deeply lobed, spiny leaves with pale woolly undersides and purple thistle-like heads. Cultivated artichokes are close relatives and can complicate identification.
actions: Where removal is appropriate, prevent seed maturation and remove the substantial taproot as completely as practical. Wear protective gloves and revisit for regrowth.

proposedDescription: Caribbean black scale can look like a row of small dark bumps along a fruit stem or twig. Mature females develop a tough, rounded covering with an H-shaped ridge; younger scales are paler and less distinctive. This sap-feeding insect uses many plants, including citrus, mango and guava. On citrus, its sugary honeydew supports sooty mold that can reduce fruit quality. Tiny natural enemies help limit populations, making a close inspection more useful than an automatic spray.
identification: Mature females are roughly 3–5 mm long, dark brown to black and hemispherical, with an H-shaped ridge. Immatures lack the clear ridge; confirm similar soft scales with an extension specialist.
actions: Inspect incoming plants and infested twigs. Preserve natural enemies; a neat round exit hole may indicate a beneficial wasp. Seek crop-specific advice before treating.

proposedDescription: Caribbean fruit fly is a yellow-brown fly whose patterned wings offer a useful first clue to its identity. Females place eggs beneath the skin of mature or overripe fruit, and the pale larvae feed inside before dropping to the soil to pupate. Guava, loquat and many other cultivated or wild fruits can serve as hosts. Because related fruit flies look similar and have different management implications, a suspected find deserves expert identification before fruit is moved.
identification: Brown S-shaped markings cross otherwise clear wings; a dark spot occurs near the rear of the thorax. White, legless larvae inside fruit are not enough for species identification.
actions: Photograph the fly and affected fruit, keep suspect fruit contained, and contact the local plant-health or agricultural office for identification and disposal guidance before transporting it.

proposedDescription: Silver trumpet tree pairs golden, funnel-shaped flowers with foliage that catches the light in a silvery sheen. Native to South America, it is planted as a warm-climate ornamental and may lose some or all of its leaves seasonally. The leaves spread from a single point like fingers, while mature capsules split to release winged seeds. Several yellow-flowered trumpet trees share this general silhouette, so the smooth leaflet edges and tiny surface scales are useful details to check.
identification: Opposite leaves have five to seven leaflets with entire edges and fine scales. Golden flowers form terminal clusters; dark mature capsules contain flattened, winged seeds. Other yellow trumpet trees may have toothed, visibly hairy leaflets.
actions: Photograph a full leaf, leaflet edges, flowers and capsules for identification. Check local planting guidance and monitor seedlings around ornamental trees before assuming they need removal.

proposedDescription: Small white flower clusters make bur parsley easy to overlook until its hooked fruits catch your attention. This annual has finely divided leaves and only a few rays in each flower cluster. It belongs to the flora of Europe, northern Africa and parts of Asia, where it often grows in dry cultivated ground and field margins. Its conservation context matters: Switzerland regards it as vulnerable. A plant found among crops is therefore not automatically a candidate for removal.
identification: Twice- or three-times-divided leaves, small white umbels with few rays, and fruits about 6–12 mm long bearing rows of hooked spines. Mature fruit is important for separating similar carrot-family plants.
actions: Record mature fruits and site, then confirm identification and local status. Avoid moving hooked fruits on clothing or equipment; do not remove plants solely because they grow in a field.

proposedDescription: Carrotwood’s glossy, leathery leaflets give this evergreen tree a tidy appearance, but its orange capsules reveal the feature that helps it travel: dark seeds wrapped in a bright aril that attracts birds. It is native to coastal eastern Australia, including rainforest near the sea and estuaries. In Florida, escaped trees invade a wide range of habitats and alter the understory. Young seedlings are much easier to tackle than the established trees they can become.
identification: Leaves are compound, usually with four to twelve leathery leaflets. Woody, yellow-orange capsules split into three sections to expose shiny black seeds with yellow-red coverings; inner bark can be orange.
actions: In invaded areas, pull small seedlings with their roots and contain seed pods. Arrange suitable professional treatment for larger trees and continue checking for bird-dispersed seedlings.

proposedDescription: The casemaking clothes moth’s most revealing sign is often a tiny moving case rather than a moth. Its caterpillar builds a portable shelter from silk and fibers, feeding on vulnerable animal-based materials such as wool as it carries the case along. The adult is a small, buff moth with narrow, fringed wings and dark forewing spots. Stored textiles and the sheltered undersides of wool rugs deserve attention, especially when they have gone undisturbed for a long time.
identification: Look for a caterpillar inside a portable silk-and-fiber case and a buff adult with three dark forewing spots. Webbing clothes moth larvae feed in attached silk tubes instead of carrying a case.
actions: Inspect affected textiles and nearby storage. Clean items using suitable laundering or dry-cleaning methods, vacuum rug edges and storage areas, and store clean woolens in sealed containers.

proposedDescription: Spectacular cassia earns its common name with broad clusters of bright yellow flowers above a rounded crown. This tropical American tree has compound leaves and long pods that darken as they mature. Its appeal as an ornamental has carried it beyond its native range; in parts of East Africa and India, it has spread into forest edges, gaps and degraded land. Dense growth can hinder forest recovery, so seedlings near vulnerable habitat merit attention before they become seed-bearing trees.
identification: Compound leaves bear several pairs of leaflets; terminal clusters hold yellow flowers with unequal petals. Long, hanging, cylindrical or slightly flattened pods turn dark.
actions: Where it is invasive, identify and remove small seedlings before seed set, contain pods, and monitor regrowth. Established trees near forest habitat require a coordinated local management plan.

proposedDescription: Cassava is a tropical crop grown for its large, starch-rich storage roots, also familiar as the source of tapioca. Above ground, it forms a woody shrub with long-stalked, deeply divided leaves and milky sap. Farmers commonly propagate it from stem cuttings, a useful reminder that discarded stems can remain planting material. Although cassava is an important food plant, its raw parts contain toxins and require proper processing; the appearance of an edible crop does not make it safe to sample.
identification: A woody shrub with alternate, long-stalked leaves divided into narrow lobes, milky sap and thickened storage roots. Do not taste plant material to confirm identification.
actions: Keep discarded stem cuttings out of natural areas and waterways. Use established food-safety guidance for processing cultivated cassava; do not eat raw roots or leaves.

proposedDescription: Castor bean is hard to miss: huge, star-shaped leaves rise on fast-growing stems, followed by clusters of prickly capsules. In warm climates it can become a substantial shrub, while frost-prone gardens often grow it as an annual. Escaped plants favor disturbed ground and waterways, and mature capsules scatter seeds that can establish new plants. Those attractive, mottled seeds are highly poisonous, so this is a plant to identify visually and keep away from children and animals.
identification: Large, glossy leaves have pointed lobes and toothed edges. Flower spikes bear petal-less flowers; rounded, spiny capsules contain smooth mottled seeds. Leaf and stem colors range from green to reddish purple.
actions: Avoid touching or collecting seeds. Wear gloves for necessary handling, prevent capsules from maturing, and obtain local disposal advice for unwanted plants. Keep children, pets and livestock away.

proposedDescription: Cat’s-claw creeper climbs with tiny, three-pronged hooks that grip bark and other supports. Its yellow trumpet flowers may look inviting, but the woody vine can spread across forest floors and climb over trees, smothering vegetation in invaded areas. Underground tubers make it persistent after the visible stems are cut. Winged seeds travel by wind and water, while detached stems and tubers can also restart growth. Early identification is especially valuable around streambanks and woodland edges.

actions: Remove small seedlings with their underground tubers where feasible, contain fragments and seed capsules, and revisit for regrowth. Have climbing infestations assessed before attempting to pull heavy vines from trees.

proposedDescription: Life plant has an unusual way of making a new generation: tiny plantlets can grow from the scalloped margins of its fleshy leaves, particularly after a leaf falls. This Madagascar succulent becomes an upright, shrubby perennial, with simple lower leaves and divided leaves farther up the stems. Drooping, bell-shaped flowers hang in branching clusters. identification: Smooth fleshy leaves have scalloped margins; upper leaves commonly divide into several oval leaflets. Look for small marginal plantlets and hanging bell-shaped flowers. Bryophyllum pinnatum is a widely used synonym.
actions: Collect dropped leaves and plantlets when containing or removing it, and keep garden waste out of natural areas. Keep plants and trimmings away from grazing animals; do not use them as food or home remedies.

proposedDescription: Catnip’s gray-green, aromatic leaves are familiar to many cat owners, but this mint-family perennial also attracts a lively mix of flower visitors. Native to Europe and Asia, it has naturalized widely in temperate regions, especially along roadsides and field margins. proposedDescription: Caucasian bluestem forms dense clumps of pale green grass that turn straw-colored as they mature. proposedDescription: Colombian datura virus can hide in an apparently healthy angel’s trumpet, then show itself as pale mottling, wrinkled leaves or stunted growth. Brugmansia plants are important hosts, and moving infected cuttings helps carry the virus between collections. Aphids and transferred plant sap can spread it too. Related ornamental and crop plants can also be infected, including tomato. Because these symptoms overlap with other problems and some infected plants show none, reliable identification depends on laboratory testing.
identification: Look for irregular light-and-dark leaf mosaics, yellow flecks, vein banding, wrinkling or reduced growth on susceptible plants. These signs are not diagnostic, and symptomless Brugmansia can carry the virus.
actions: Stop sharing or propagating suspect plants and contact a plant diagnostic laboratory. Use tested healthy stock for propagation, prevent sap transfer between plants, and follow diagnostic advice for removing confirmed infected stock.

proposedDescription: Cedar wattle is a tall Australian tree with unusually large leaflets for a feathery-leaved acacia. Sprays of pale yellow or cream flower balls appear above the foliage, followed by flat pods. In its native New South Wales range, it grows in rainforest and wetter eucalypt forest. Planting has carried it farther afield: it can escape into adjacent bushland and is documented as naturalized in South Africa. Its location matters when deciding whether a seedling belongs or needs attention.
identification: Twice-divided leaves have several pairs of branches carrying lance-shaped leaflets commonly 2–5 cm long. Look for pale spherical flower heads, flat pods, and dark, deeply fissured bark at the base of mature trees.
actions: Record leaflets, pods and the planting context. Outside its native range, monitor nearby bushland for seedlings and seek local management advice; arrange professional assessment before removing large trees.

proposedDescription: Greater celandine brings small yellow flowers to shady edges, gardens, and disturbed woodland. This leafy herb lives for more than one season or behaves as a biennial, spreading readily by seed where conditions suit it. Its deeply divided leaves and orange-yellow sap help separate it from other yellow-flowered plants. Originally from Eurasia, it has become established beyond its native range. The sap can irritate skin, so this is a plant to recognize without breaking its stems by hand.
identification: Look for clusters of four-petaled yellow flowers, lobed leaves, and long, slender seed capsules. Do not deliberately expose skin to the sap.
actions: Wear gloves when removing small unwanted plants, and work before they set seed. Recheck the area for seedlings.
researchNotes: Synthesized morphology and garden behavior with Kew's range and life-form account. Kept greater celandine distinct from lesser celandine; no unsupported nationwide impact claim.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Chelidonium majus

claims: Yellow four-petaled flowers; divided leaves; irritating colored sap; rapid reseeding.
Accepted Eurasian herb with introduced populations outside its native range.

proposedDescription: This cellar spider belongs to the long-legged spiders that hang beneath loose webs in sheltered corners. Pholcus manueli has been recorded in cellars and other buildings, including a garage from which it was first described. Although its name was established from American specimens, the World Spider Catalog treats it as an Asian species introduced to the United States. Several cellar spiders look similar, so a web in a basement is a useful clue, not enough to identify this particular species.
identification: Long, thin legs and an inverted position in an irregular web suggest a cellar spider. Species-level identification needs an expert examination.
actions: Photograph the spider and its web if documenting a sighting. Seek identification before treating a familiar house spider as this species.
researchNotes: USDA field observations independently support building habitat; Bern's catalog resolves accepted identity and introduced status. Family traits are presented as family traits, not unique diagnostic characters.

sources.title: USDA Forest Service: Spiders of Milbridge, Maine

claims: Pholcid web and leg traits; P. manueli collected in a cellar and government building.
Accepted species with Asian distribution and introduced United States status.

proposedDescription: Centipedegrass is the pale-green, low-growing lawn grass often planted in warm parts of the country. It creeps across the soil on aboveground runners, gradually forming a coarse-textured turf rather than an upright clump. Its leaves alternate along the runners, giving them the appearance that inspired its common name. This grass is adapted to acidic, relatively low-fertility soils. Because it is widely cultivated, a patch beside a lawn should be described in that context rather than automatically labeled a harmful invasion.
identification: Look for light-green blades alternating along creeping runners and a slender, single seed spike. St. Augustinegrass has opposite leaves.
actions: Keep planted turf within its intended area. For unwanted patches, confirm the grass before selecting a removal method with local extension advice.
researchNotes: Both university accounts support identification and turf ecology. Deliberately avoided equating cultivation or escape with demonstrated ecological damage.

sources.title: UF/IFAS: Identification of Common Florida Lawn Grasses

claims: Warm-season turf; aboveground stolons; alternate leaves; acid low-fertility soils.
Centipedegrass blade, sheath, growth-habit and seedhead characteristics.

proposedDescription: Centipede tongavine is a tropical climbing plant whose leaves change dramatically as it grows. Young shoots creep or climb with relatively simple leaves; older shoots supported by a tree or another surface can produce much larger, deeply divided leaves. Aerial roots help the vine hold on as it climbs. Native across parts of Asia and the Pacific, it is grown ornamentally beyond that range. Its changing leaf shape makes identifying mature and juvenile plants together especially useful.
identification: Compare young and mature leaves and look for clasping aerial roots. Deeply divided mature leaves differ from the simpler juvenile foliage.
actions: Keep cultivated vines contained and do not discard living cuttings in natural areas. Photograph several growth stages for identification.
researchNotes: Kew and NParks support identity, life form and morphology. Excluded the older GISD account of E. pinnatum cv. Aureum to avoid transferring golden-pothos impacts to this species.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Epipremnum pinnatum

claims: Root-climbing habit and contrasting juvenile and mature foliage.
Accepted tropical climber with Asian-Pacific native range and introduced records.

proposedDescription: This microscopic diatom is known from freshwater plankton and is associated with the smaller freshwater forms of Actinocyclus normanii. Viewed through a microscope, its round silica shell has a patterned surface of pores that specialists use for identification. Its history in the Great Lakes is less straightforward than an introduction date might suggest: older sediment evidence has raised questions about whether it arrived recently at all. Even the boundary between named forms is uncertain, making careful identification more useful than a simple invasive label.
identification: Identification requires microscopy of the circular valve, pore arrangement, and specialized structures. Small size alone does not securely identify the named form.
actions: Have a qualified diatom specialist examine samples. Record sampling details; do not attempt species-specific treatment based on water appearance.
researchNotes: Research gap: queue spelling f. subsala differs from f. subsalsa in the reviewed accounts, and Diatoms.org questions a clear boundary between forms. Keep ID unchanged pending taxonomic reconciliation; native status remains uncertain.

sources.title: Diatoms of North America: Actinocyclus normanii
USGS Great Lakes account: Actinocyclus normanii f. subsalsa

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Diatoms of North America editorial team
claims: Circular pore-patterned valves; small freshwater form; uncertainty in form separation.
Freshwater plankton ecology and uncertainty over introduction history from sediment evidence.

proposedDescription: Skeletonema potamos is a tiny diatom that drifts in fresh and slightly brackish water, often as short chains of cells. Its delicate silica walls are so small that it can be overlooked even under a light microscope. Researchers studying the Danube found that it became a larger part of the river's plankton community as water temperatures rose. Its original range remains uncertain, and finding it in a water sample does not by itself establish a harmful bloom or a recent introduction.
identification: Specialists look for very small cylindrical cells joined in chains by marginal structures. Reliable identification may require detailed microscopy.
actions: Document the waterbody and sampling conditions and seek specialist confirmation. Avoid transporting untreated water or wet equipment between waterbodies.
researchNotes: Combined USGS ecological context with the independent Danube study's original morphology and long-term observations. The warming relationship is regional and correlational, not a universal impact claim.

sources.title: USGS Great Lakes account: Skeletonema potamos
Duleba and colleagues: Skeletonema potamos in the River Danube

claims: Small chain-forming diatom in freshwater and brackish habitats; uncertain original range.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Duleba et al. Danube research team
claims: Original cell morphology; increasing relative abundance correlated with warming during 1979–2012.

proposedDescription: Cereal cyst nematode is a microscopic roundworm that feeds inside the roots of wheat, barley, oats, and other grasses. Damaged roots have more difficulty supplying the plant with water and nutrients, which can leave uneven patches of weak or stunted crop. After a female dies, her hardened body becomes a cyst that shelters eggs in the soil. Those persistent cysts make the problem longer-lived than one growing season, while the symptoms above ground can easily be mistaken for other crop stresses.
identification: Stunting and poor patches are warning signs, not a diagnosis. Root and soil samples need laboratory examination to distinguish related cyst nematodes.
actions: Ask an agricultural diagnostic service how to sample affected patches. Use confirmed species identity to guide crop rotation and resistant-variety choices.
researchNotes: UC Davis biology and Oregon State's regional management synthesis independently support the draft. H. filipjevi is a distinct look-alike; resistance and diagnosis should not be generalized across species.

sources.title: Oregon State Extension: Cereal Cyst Nematodes

claims: Cereal root parasite; life cycle and persistent egg-bearing cysts.
Root damage and nonspecific crop symptoms; species diagnosis informs rotations and resistance.

proposedDescription: The cereal leaf beetle is a small insect with metallic blue wing covers and an orange-red area behind its head. Its larvae are easier to notice by what they leave behind: narrow strips of damaged tissue on cereal and grass leaves. A dark coating of their own waste often hides the larvae's pale bodies. Heavy feeding can reduce the leaf area a grain crop needs to fill its seeds, but natural enemies also help keep populations in check, making field monitoring important.
identification: Look for blue-winged, orange-thoraxed adults and waste-coated larvae feeding along leaves. Similar Oulema beetles may need expert separation.
actions: Inspect crop leaves and consult local extension thresholds before treatment. Preserve beneficial insects rather than spraying automatically after a single sighting.
researchNotes: USU supports feeding, life cycle and crop management; the UK recording scheme independently supports adult morphology and look-alike limitations. Avoided assigning all striped leaf damage to this species.

sources.title: Utah State University Extension: Cereal Leaf Beetle

claims: Adult and larval appearance; leaf injury; monitoring and natural enemies.
Adult size and coloration; close similarity to O. rufocyanea.

proposedDescription: Cereal rye is an upright annual grass grown for grain, forage, and soil cover. Its tall stems carry dense, bristly seed heads that may lean as they mature, while a network of roots helps hold the soil. It is a familiar agricultural plant that can also appear outside the places where it was sown. Despite the similar name, cereal rye is not the same as the ryegrasses used in many lawns and pastures. Identifying the seed head helps tell those grasses apart.
identification: Look for a dense, elongated grain head with conspicuous awns and flat leaves. Confirm the whole plant rather than relying on the name rye.
actions: Where rye is unwanted, document whether it is planted or growing independently. Ask local extension about preventing further seed production.
researchNotes: Two university accounts support crop uses, growth form and identification. No unsupported ecosystem-damage claim was inferred from its presence in the editorial queue.

claims: Annual grain, forage and cover crop; root and growth characteristics.
Erect grass with long-awned, dense seed spikes and flat leaves.

proposedDescription: Cerulean flaxlily forms clumps of long, sword-shaped leaves, with small pale flowers followed by glossy blue berries. Although its foliage may look grasslike at first glance, it spreads from underground rhizomes and carries its flowers on branching stalks above the leaves. Birds can disperse its fruit. Native across parts of the Old World tropics, it has also been grown as an ornamental. In Florida, UF/IFAS assesses it as invasive, so its attractive appearance should not be the only consideration when choosing a landscape plant.
identification: Look for leaves arranged in two ranks, pale flowers with prominent yellow-orange anthers, and shiny blue berries.
actions: In Florida, follow UF/IFAS advice against its use. Elsewhere, check local guidance before planting and prevent unwanted fruit or rhizome spread.
researchNotes: NParks supports morphology and dispersal; UF/IFAS supplies a separate Florida risk assessment. The Florida conclusion is explicitly regional, not a nationwide legal claim.

claims: Rhizomatous clumps; swordlike foliage; blue berries and bird dispersal.
Completed Florida assessment classifies the plant as Invasive (No Uses).

proposedDescription: Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus affects crops in the cucumber family, including cucumbers, melons, pumpkins, and squash. Infected plants may develop mottled or distorted leaves, poor growth, or damaged fruit, although symptoms vary with the crop and conditions. The virus travels with contaminated seed and plant material and can also move on hands, tools, and other surfaces. That combination makes clean planting material and careful hygiene especially important in gardens, greenhouses, and farms where susceptible crops are grown.
identification: Mosaic-patterned leaves and abnormal fruit can suggest a virus, but laboratory testing is needed to distinguish CGMMV from other problems.
actions: Pause movement of suspect plants and contact a plant diagnostic laboratory or extension service. Follow their sampling and disinfection instructions.
researchNotes: APHIS and Agriculture Victoria support hosts, symptoms and transmission. Kept Australian legal/reporting requirements out of US guidance and distinguished suspicion from a confirmed diagnosis.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: Cucumber Green Mottle Mosaic Virus
Agriculture Victoria: Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus

claims: CGMMV affects cucurbit crops and can cause serious crop damage.
Variable symptoms; contaminated seed, material and contact transmission; testing and hygiene.

proposedDescription: Chamberbitter is a small warm-season annual that can appear among garden plants, in lawns, and in other disturbed ground. Its neat rows of little leaves make a branch look like a miniature mimosa leaf, but those are individual leaves rather than leaflets. Turn a branch over and the round seed capsules underneath become a useful clue. Plants can make seed while still quite small, which is why repeatedly mowing the tops may leave the next generation ready to grow.
identification: Look beneath the leafy branches for small, rounded capsules on very short stalks. Long-stalked capsules suggest a different Phyllanthus.
actions: Pull small plants before seeds mature and use suitable mulch in beds. Mowing alone may not prevent seed production.
researchNotes: NC State botanical characters resolve the misleading compound-leaf appearance; UF/IFAS contributes independent garden-management guidance. Kept P. tenellus distinct.

claims: Two-ranked simple leaves and short-stalked capsules distinguish chamberbitter.
Warm-season annual; seeds while small; hand removal and mulch; mowing limitations.

proposedDescription: Chameleon plant is a spreading perennial with heart-shaped leaves and a strong scent when its foliage is crushed. Garden forms may have brightly patterned leaves, but the plant can also be plain green. What look like four white petals surround a short spike of tiny flowers. It thrives in moist ground and spreads through creeping underground stems, which can carry it well beyond a garden bed. Those hidden stems also make an established patch more persistent than its soft leaves might suggest.
identification: Look for heart-shaped leaves and a short flower spike surrounded by four white bracts. Leaf coloration varies among garden forms.
actions: Avoid planting it beside natural wetlands. Where removing a patch, collect creeping stems carefully and monitor for regrowth rather than only clipping leaves.
researchNotes: NC State and RHS independently support moist-site growth, spreading habit and flower structure. White structures are bracts; no nationwide invasive designation asserted.

claims: Heart-shaped foliage; scented leaves; white bracts; aggressive rhizome spread.
Spreading perennial suited to moist or boggy ground; flowers and foliage.

proposedDescription: Chandelier plant is a succulent with narrow, mottled leaves and clusters of hanging orange-red flowers. Tiny plantlets develop at the leaf tips, detach, and become new plants, helping explain its other name, mother of millions. This Madagascar native has been grown ornamentally and can establish in warm, open habitats beyond gardens. Its ability to reproduce from small pieces makes garden waste an important concern. The plant is poisonous to livestock and pets, so identification matters around grazing land and homes.
identification: Look for slender, grooved leaves with a few teeth and plantlets near their tips. Related mother-of-millions hybrids have broader leaves.
actions: Keep animals away from the plant and collect fallen plantlets when removing it. Follow local disposal guidance; do not dump living material outdoors.
researchNotes: NC State morphology and NSW field guidance agree on plantlets, toxicity and spread. Kept the broader-leaved hybrid separate and omitted Southern Hemisphere flowering dates.

claims: Madagascar succulent; narrow leaves, terminal plantlets and pendant flowers; toxicity.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: New South Wales Department of Primary Industries
claims: Plantlet and fragment spread; livestock risk; identification from related hybrid.

proposedDescription: Changing forget-me-not earns its name as its tiny flowers age from pale yellow or cream to blue. Several colors can appear on the same curling flower cluster, a helpful detail when this small plant blends into grassy ground. It is a hairy annual with slender stems and narrow leaves, originally from Europe and now established elsewhere. Roadsides, ditches, open pasture, and other disturbed places can provide suitable habitat. A close view of the flowers is much more useful for identification than a distant patch of blue.
identification: Look for different flower colors on one cluster, small five-lobed corollas, and hooked hairs on the calyx. A hand lens helps.
actions: Photograph fresh and older flowers together. Confirm identification before removing forget-me-nots, since a common name can cover several species.
researchNotes: Independent New Zealand and British Columbia floras agree on color change and morphology. No unsupported claim of severe ecological harm was added.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Myosotis discolor

claims: Annual hairy herb; cream or yellow corollas become blue; open pasture habitat.
European introduction; disturbed moist sites; flower, leaf and calyx characters.

proposedDescription: The channeled apple snail is a large freshwater snail that grazes on aquatic plants and can damage crops grown in wet fields. Its rounded shell has deep grooves between the coils, while conspicuous pink egg masses are laid above the waterline. Originally South American, it has been moved to other regions through human activity. In Hawaii, it became a serious pest of wetland taro. Several apple snails look alike, so shell color or a pink egg mass alone cannot settle the species identity.
identification: Photograph the shell, grooves, and egg mass without moving them. Expert examination may be needed to separate it from other introduced apple snails.
actions: Do not release aquarium snails or move snails, eggs, or contaminated plants between sites. Ask local aquatic or agricultural authorities about suspected populations.
researchNotes: EPPO supports current diagnosis and biology; the Hawaii chapter provides independent agricultural observations. Older P. insularum/maculata confusion was not used to assign records or impacts.

claims: Freshwater plant feeder; shell and egg morphology; identification limits among apple snails.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Levin et al. Hawaii research team
claims: Introductions associated with food production and major damage to Hawaiian wetland taro.

proposedDescription: Charlock mustard, also called wild mustard, is an annual plant with clusters of bright yellow, four-petaled flowers. It often grows in cultivated fields and other disturbed ground, where its broad leaves and upright stems compete with crops for space and resources. Long seed pods follow the flowers, and seeds left in the soil can supply later generations. It belongs to the same plant family as many familiar vegetables, so recognizing its leaves, flowers, and pods together is more reliable than identifying it by color alone.
identification: Look for four yellow petals, rough or hairy foliage, and elongated pods. Other yellow-flowered mustards can be very similar.
actions: Remove unwanted plants before mature pods release seed. In crop fields, use local weed-management advice and monitor for later seedlings.
researchNotes: Cornell's weed account and NC State's botanical profile support an agricultural-weed description. Persistence is discussed without assigning a universal seed-longevity figure or legal status.

claims: Annual crop weed; seed persistence; management before seed return.
Yellow four-petaled flowers, hairy foliage and seed pods in disturbed habitats.

proposedDescription: The charru mussel is a small, thin-shelled mussel found in estuaries, lagoons, and other sheltered coastal waters. Its shell can range from greenish to nearly black, with a purple inner surface. It filters suspended food from the water and can gather on shells, roots, docks, and aquaculture structures. Introduced populations have become locally abundant, but abundance alone does not measure their effects: field research has found that competition with other mussels needs more careful study than some broad claims suggest.
identification: Look for a relatively smooth, thin shell with a purple interior. Native and other introduced mussels require expert comparison.
actions: Photograph suspect mussels in place and report unfamiliar fouling to local marine-resource staff. Avoid moving live mussels or fouled equipment between waters.
researchNotes: Smithsonian supports morphology and ecology; the independent 2023 Thailand survey, published in 2024, supports dense populations while cautioning about unproven displacement. M. charruana is an older name used in sources.

sources.title: Wells and colleagues: Charru mussel in the upper Gulf of Thailand

claims: Shell characters; estuarine habitat; suspension feeding and attached-substrate records.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Wells et al. Thailand field survey team
claims: Dense estuary and aquaculture populations; limited measured spread; uncertain competitive displacement.

proposedDescription: Chayote is a vigorous climbing vine best known for its pale-green, pear-shaped vegetable, also called mirliton or vegetable pear. The fruit contains a single large seed, and the vine uses supports to lift its cucumber-like leaves and developing crop above the ground. Separate male and female flowers grow on the same plant and attract pollinators. This tropical American crop is cultivated in warm regions around the world. Its presence in a garden is therefore different from a vine growing independently beyond cultivation.
identification: Look for a climbing cucurbit with cucumber-like leaves and a ridged or sometimes prickly, pear-shaped fruit containing one seed.
actions: Keep cultivated vines on suitable supports and within the growing area. Document escaped growth separately from deliberately planted crops.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS and the Indian Institute of Science support morphology and cultivation. Retained the queue's Sechium name; Sicyos edulis is noted in the flora as its basionym. No US ecological harm assumed.

sources.title: Indian Institute of Science: Sechium edule

claims: Climbing crop; separate male and female flowers; pear-shaped single-seeded fruit.
Perennial climber; hairy leaves, greenish flowers and cultivated edible fruit.

proposedDescription: Cheatgrass is an annual grass that often starts growing in fall, spends winter as a small plant, and produces seed early the following season. Its soft, hairy leaves give way to drooping, bristly seed heads, then dry vegetation as the season warms. In many western landscapes, this early-drying growth adds fine fuel between larger plants and can help fires spread. Repeated disturbance can favor more cheatgrass, making prevention of seed production and recovery of perennial vegetation important parts of long-term management.
identification: Look for soft hairs on the leaves and sheaths, a prominent membranous ligule, and nodding seed heads with long awns.
actions: Clean seeds from boots and equipment. For established patches, plan control before seed maturity and pair it with recovery of suitable perennial cover.
researchNotes: Illinois identification and Montana management accounts independently support the draft. Fire effects are framed for affected western landscapes, not every occurrence.

sources.title: Montana State Extension: Cheatgrass identification, biology and integrated management

claims: Hairy annual grass; drooping awned heads; early drying and western fire concern.
Seasonal life cycle; integrated control before seed production and perennial vegetation recovery.
